Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

ABSTRACT
Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the 
lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest 
social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case. In 600 Indonesian 
villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much 
a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-
assessed welfare. Targeting consumption misses 77% of households with the highest marginal 
social valuation. Targeting self-assessed welfare misses 57%. Even targeting those the community 
ranks worst off in levels, not margins, misses 25%. Divergences between different notions of 
neediness are statistically predictable. In a randomized controlled trial, proxy means tests best 
target consumption, self-targeting ordeals capture self-assessed welfare levels, and community 
targeting comes closest to marginal social valuation. Targeting strategies inescapably embed 
normative stances.

TARGET WHAT? 1
“The distinctive characteristic of a problem of social policy is indeed the fact that
it cannot be resolved merely on the basis of purely technical considerations which
assume already settled ends. ”
–Max Weber, The “Objectivity” of Knowledge in Social Science and Social Policy
1. Introduction
Most social programs are intended to be targeted to the ‘neediest,’ but it is not
necessarily clear what that means. Is the relevant target the household with the
lowest level of consumption or the one who will benefit the most from the transfer?
And when we consider who will benefit the most, whose point of view do we have in
mind? For example, even parents often have a different view of consumption options
for their children than the children themselves. Might communities feel the same way
about their members? While a libertarian might say that the community’s views are
irrelevant, the community might want a say.
In this paper, we argue that these distinctions are largely ignored in current policy
practice, based on the assumption that they are more or less the same. Yet they
represent fundamentally different normative stances. We develop a framework that
allows us to probe these issues and their implications for the choice of targeting meth-
ods, and examine them empirically. We use unique data that we collected from over
5,500 villagers in Indonesia, which asks each respondent not only about their con-
sumption and their self-reported well-being, but also about who in their community
has the lowest level of welfare, and crucially, who will be assisted the most by a social
transfer. Our survey shows these notions of need are distinct. An RCT covering 600
villages shows which notions different targeting methods reflect in practice.
There is a reason why these concerns are not more salient in discussions about
targeting. The standard framework assumes a social planner who allocates benefits
to maximize a utilitarian aggregate social welfare function under the assumption that
while households may be richer or poorer, their preferences are the same. Specifically,
suppose that each household i has a utility function u(ci,1,ci,2,...,c i,n) of different
consumption choices cij, increasing in each good j and jointly concave, which they
maximize subject to budget constraint ∑ jcij =Ci. This generates a concave indirect
utility functionU(Ci). The utilitarian social maximand is ∑ iU(Ci+di), wheredi = 1
if the household gets a small government benefit and 0 otherwise. This tells us that
the benefits should be targeted to those with the highest U′(Ci). Under the standard
assumption that U is identical across households and concave, those with the largest
U′(Ci) are the same as those with the lowest U(Ci), and are also the same as those
TARGET WHAT? 2
with the lowest Ci. This is very convenient since, in this special case, the utilitarian
prescription is to give assistance to the very poorest, aligning it with a Rawlsian
concern for the worst off, despite their different rationales (Rawls, 1971). 1
Unfortunately, this elegant resolution relies heavily on U not varying a lot from
one person to another. The first empirical finding of this paper is that this does not
seem to be true. In our survey, we solicited both household consumption Ci and self-
assessed welfare Ui(Ci).2 When we compare self-reported welfare with consumption
at the household level, we find that higher consumption often does not imply higher
well-being. Although they co-move, the raw correlation is only 0.33. As such, very
few of those targeted based on Ui(Ci) will be chosen based on Ci, which makes it
clear that once we have this type of heterogeneity, it is no longer obvious that one
should necessarily target the poorest. 3
One reason why consumption and utility diverge is that different people have dif-
ferent needs. For example, someone who needs expensive, life-saving medical care
may have a higher marginal utility than a similar-income, healthy individual. 4 This
suggests focusing directly on marginal utilityU′ i(Ci) as the single criterion for allocat-
ing benefits; that would capture the idea, for example, that those with higher needs
for medical expenses value extra consumption spending more.
However, one immediately runs into multiple challenges. One is that it is not obvi-
ous how to truthfully elicit marginal utility U′ i(Ci) in a high-stakes setting. But even
more fundamentally, it seems to us that most people—including many who describe
themselves as utilitarians, and certainly including Rawlsians and prioritarians—would
balk at giving social benefits to Elon Musk, even if he provided convincing evidence
that the benefit would increase his own utility a great deal. (Here, Musk would effec-
tively be Nozick’s “utility monster” or Sen’s “pleasure wizard”, who is unusual in his
ability to convert money into utility (Nozick, 1974; Sen, 1980): Musk spent two years
litigating, after all, to restore a 2018 stock-option package worth roughly $56 billion

TARGET WHAT? 5
It turns out that the divergence between Vi(Ci) and V′ i (Ci) is predictable from
observables. For instance, widows are assigned high V′ i (Ci) relative to their Vi(Ci).
More generally, we can reject that the relationship between each alternative measure
and a set of observables is the same ( p < 0.001). The presence of these distinct
predictable patterns suggests that the gap between these two measures of need is not
just a result of unthinking judgments, but a reflection of specific social mores.
These distinctions make it obvious that a policymaker cannot avoid taking a nor-
mative stance. Any targeting strategy can be thought of as optimizing a normative
objective, so the question is what it values; since these different notions of welfare pick
up different households, one must ultimately make a normative judgment. A natural
(and non-paternalistic) option is to respect the community’s judgment and implement
V′ i (Ci).7 This is appealing: distributive judgments may depend on locally shared un-
derstandings of what assistance is for and who needs it most (Walzer, 1983), so why
should we privilege the views of an external actor—and doubly so when the commu-
nity exhibits consensus? At the same time, the policymaker may want to preserve the
community’sV′ i (Ci), subject to moral side-constraints, refusing to implement racist,
sexist, casteist, or otherwise odious components of that judgment. 8
One diagnostic to test for this is to examine the relationship between V′ i (Ci) and
the types of characteristics a planner may find objectionable. In our setting, when
we examine the relationship between V′ i (Ci) and various characteristics Xi, we do
not find evidence that V′ i (Ci) is systematically lower for ethnic minority households
conditional on Xi, suggesting that this may not be a first-order issue here. But we
return below to what to do in other settings that may exhibit more of these challenges.
Thus far we have investigated different notions of welfare. What does the existence
of these large wedges – between Ci and Ui(Ci), between Ui(Ci) and Vi(Ci), and be-
tweenVi(Ci) and V′ i (Ci) – imply for the design of targeting schemes that determine
who receives assistance in practice? There are three standard ways of targeting: (1)
directly measuring consumption (or more commonly, predicting consumption based
on a Proxy Means Test or PMT) and targeting lowest Ci; (2) asking the community

At a purely conceptual level, one implication of our first set of results is that even
a perfectly implemented PMT targeting the poorest (lowest Ci) does not necessarily
target the neediest as measured by either V′ i (Ci), Vi(Ci), or Ui(Ci). A second impli-

ones that the community perceives to be the neediest. While one would expect these
methods to target different concepts of need based on first principles, it is possible
that the real world implementations end up wiping out these differences.
The final set of empirical exercises studies which targeting methods weigh which
notions of need. In a randomized controlled trial allocating real transfers – a rollout
of the Indonesian conditional cash transfer program, worth over USD 150 per year for
6 years – 600 Indonesian villages were randomized to one of three targeting methods:
traditional PMT, self-targeting based on a small sign-up cost, and community tar-
geting (see Alatas et al., 2016b; Sumarto et al., 2025). We find that the PMT clearly
reached more lowCi households than the other methods, while the self-selection mech-
anism targeted low Ui(Ci) households, and the community-based approach was best
at finding low Vi(Ci) and high V′ i (Ci) households. Moreover, in each case targeting
works best for the most needy as per the corresponding measure–exactly the set of
households we would expect to be selected for social transfers under each approach.

to adapt the ideas of tagging based on observables from Akerlof (1978) but aimed at
V′ i . This has two potential advantages. First, practically, measuring V′ i (Ci) requires
conducting a community assessment everywhere, which involves a very different lo-
gistical strategy than that done for existing PMTs; by contrast, PMTs already do
the work of measuring Xi for every household in a country, so one could just change
the prediction function to obtain ˆV′ i instead of ˆCi. Second, as discussed above, to
the extent that the social planner agrees with some, but not all, of the determinants

5.3. An Alternative Implementation: MSV-PMT. The results thus far show
that marginal social valuation is distinct from other concepts. Among the three
targeting methods we consider, community targeting is the only one that puts sub-
stantial weight on marginal social valuation above and beyond the other measures of
need. However, implementing community-based targeting is logistically challenging,
requiring community meetings everywhere. Particularly for countries that have al-
ready invested substantially in collecting the demographic characteristics Xi for the
entire population necessary for implementing a PMT, it is therefore interesting to
explore the feasibility of an alternative, novel targeting mechanism, the “ marginal
social valuation proxy-means test,” (henceforth, the ‘MSV-PMT’). The idea is to esti-
mate the marginal social valuation from observables and bypass the costs associated
with a community targeting process. As in the standard PMT, we use rank-ordered

the prediction, we use marginal social valuation. We use predicted values from this
regression to obtain ˆV ′ i , and use ˆV ′ i to assign benefits. We can compute these scores
for every household in our sample, allowing us to examine all 600 villages. As in the

We investigate who would be targeted via that MSV-PMT in the orange bars of
Figure 3. We see that the MSV-PMT stakes out a middle ground between com-

Returning to Table 5, we see similar patterns in column 8– the MSV-PMT targets
households with high V′ i (Ci) and low Vi(Ci); conditional on these values, it does
not provide “additional” aid to low consumption households. But it does so to a
lesser degree than community targeting alone when reaching low Vi(Ci) households,
suggesting that some of what is being captured by communities cannot be captured
by observablesXi. It also provides additional aid to households with low self-assessed
welfareUi(Ci) conditional on the other measures of need.
That said, relative to community targeting the MSV-PMT is potentially much more
scalable. There are no meeting costs, and it is widely understood that the cost of
proxies for these predictive exercises is low. On the other hand, we have seen that
(1) MSV-PMT exhibits a lower true positive rate relative to community targeting
for both Vi and V′ i benchmarks and (2) by definition such a predictive model can
only be applied out of sample when the new region is thought to be exchangeable
with the old. Constructing an MSV-PMT in one setting and applying it to a very
different setting would therefore only make sense if one thought that the views of the
community where the MSV-PMT is trained are valid in the areas to which it will be
applied. That is, applying our model for predicting V′ i (Ci) in Indonesia to villages
in Ghana (or even taking them from one part of the Indian state of West Bengal to
another) may be much less effective, given these villages may have different social
norms around need. To operationalize the idea of an MSV-PMT, policymakers would
need to solicit determinants ofV′ i (Ci) specific to the relevant context (and, obviously,
accept lower quality targeting if indeed V′ i or Vi is the benchmark).

6. Discussion
Targeting as a Normative Choice. Targeting requires a normative objective.
Who is “neediest” depends on whether the planner prioritizes low consumption ( Ci),
low self-assessed welfare (Ui(Ci)), low community-assessed welfare in levels (Vi(Ci)),
or a large community-assessed gain from the transfer ( V′ i (Ci)). These rankings do
not have to agree, and different targeting methods build in different notions of need-
iness. A consumption-based rule is justified by a benchmark in which households are
exchangeable at the margin conditional on consumption. An ordeal ranks households
by private net willingness to participate. This corresponds with marginal utility only
when the costs of the ordeal do not overturn the private-benefit ordering; otherwise
it corresponds to valuing households less should they happen to have higher costs
to perform the ordeal (e.g., disability, social exclusion). Community targeting likely
reflects both socially assessed welfare in levels and assessed gain from the transfer.
These distinctions matter empirically. Targeting the bottom decile of consumption
misses 77% of the households with the highest community-assessed gain from the
transfer. Evaluating a PMT against consumption is thus not equivalent to evaluating
it against the community’s social-gain ranking. None of this implies that the com-
munity ranking should bind the planner. While a community ranking may combine
local information about debt, dependency, and vulnerability, it is also possible that
it incorporates likely uses of the transfer and other social judgments that the planner
may not endorse, though we do not see evidence for this in our context. More gen-
erally, a policymaker needs to be clear about their normative stance, whatever it is:
which components of local social valuation they are willing to incorporate, and why.
The choice must be purposeful, not an accident of the targeting method. Our MSV-
PMT illustrates one strategy that could potentially be used to predict high marginal
social valuation for targeting. However, it also has tradeoffs: it places more weight
on the community’s marginal social valuation ranking than a standard PMT trained
to predict consumption, but fails to completely reproduce direct elicitation, showing
that unobservables play a major role in a local society’s normative perspective.
Implications for Impact and Algorithmic Targeting. These distinctions extend
to recent work studying how targeting should trade off baseline deprivation against
heterogeneous impacts (Haushofer et al., 2025; Bj¨ orkegren et al., 2026). Related evi-
dence on poverty traps and general-equilibrium spillovers shows why the effects of an
antipoverty intervention may be persistent, heterogeneous, and extend beyond direct

recipients (Balboni et al., 2022; Egger et al., 2022). Notice that with a common trans-
fer that raises consumption one-for-one and a common concave consumption index,
poverty targeting is ordinal: a planner only needs the ranking of baseline consump-
tion. If the planner trades impact against deprivation, the approach is cardinal. Let
b denote the common transfer and let ti = ∆Ci(b) > 0 denote the predicted con-
sumption effect used by the targeting rule. Under a benchmark that identifies social
welfare with private utility, the local welfare gain is U′ i(Ci)ti. If the planner adopts
the community’s social valuation of consumption, it is V′ i (Ci)ti. More generally, the
planner may have some∂Cϕi(Ci,zi)ti. Note that while ti are painstakingly estimated
through these efforts, ultimately the policy implications may depend as much on the
choice of welfare metric as on the precision with which ti is estimated.
The issue is not that this literature fails to specify welfare criteria. Haushofer
et al. (2025) explicitly vary the welfare function, curvature, outcome, time horizon,
and Pareto weights. Bj¨ orkegren et al. (2026) separate heterogeneous impacts from
welfare weights on people and weights on outcomes. Egger et al. (2022) likewise
distinguish an output multiplier from welfare. Butti is estimated from data, while the
choice of welfare criterion (e.g., homogeneous CARA/CRRA utility) embeds an aspect
of normative speculation. Even when welfare weights are estimated, they remain
conditional on chosen outcomes, functional forms, and restrictions on heterogeneity.
A set of cash transfer experiments in Kenya illustrates the problem. Haushofer
et al. (2025) find that the households predicted to have the largest consumption ef-
fects are not the most deprived. But in the same setting, Walker et al. (2025) find
that nearly the entire reduction in infant mortality is concentrated among very poor
households, and that mortality effects are essentially zero among groups predicted to
have the largest consumption and asset gains. This suggests that instead of map-
ping everything to consumption, as is done in practice, there is a vector of effects
that ought to be normatively considered. “Targeting impact” is incomplete until
the researcher specifies which effects count and how they are aggregated. Clearly
a one-dimensional consumption index can reweight consumption gains by baseline
consumption, but it cannot independently value child survival, disability, or vulner-
ability. (But our empirical V′ i is deliberately reduced form and permits respondents
to integrate whichever consequences they regard as relevant. It neither separately
identifies those consequences nor the weights placed on them, nor is it intended to.)

Recent innovations in prediction methods do not escape these normative issues.
Aiken et al. (2025) compare proxy means tests, community nominations, and machine-
learning predictions based on mobile-phone metadata. Their comparison defines suc-
cess relative to consumption poverty. The PMT reproduces that target most accu-
rately, while phone-based targeting can be more cost-effective under some combina-
tions of program scale, screening costs, and transfer budgets. Though these findings
establish which mechanism best implements the consumption target, as we have ar-
gued, this target may not capture the socially preferred recipient. Our MSV-PMT
shows that analogous prediction machinery can instead be trained on V′ i directly,
though unobservables limit how far this goes. There is also a question of portability.
Perhaps it is reasonable to think that a function predicting consumption is stable
across communities, but who is to say that social valuations or moral judgments are?
The issue is also not one of scaling. Algorithms scale nicely, clearly, provided the
prediction function is stable – though there is a serious question of quality of pre-
diction and stability across geographies. Eliciting rankings reflecting V′ i or utilizing
community targeting is not free either; it requires new methods that may be less light
touch than a PMT. But it need not be prohibitively expensive. In this same exper-
iment, community targeting was cheaper to administer than a scaled PMT (Alatas
et al., 2016b). And it has the advantage of potentially targeting a socially valued
goal.45 There is a bit of a blind spot at times in the literature about this trade-off.
Concluding Remarks. When a government writes down a targeting rule, it is im-
plicitly maximizing some normative objective. The policymaker’s own normative
view may or may not align with the objective being implemented – perhaps naively,
or perhaps as a deliberate second best 46 – but it is important to be clear, because it
clarifies the kind of policy one wants. Normative perspectives will also differ and, re-
specting some boundaries, there is scope for pluralism without unbounded relativism.
Communities, for instance, hold normative views of their own: they assess who gains
from a transfer, possibly in complex ways that line up with neither welfare levels nor
private preferences, and a non-paternalistic policymaker may at least want to con-
sider those assessments. We have shown that these distinctions matter empirically
and that the standard targeting methods implement different ones. Prescriptively,
then, a policymaker must be clear about what their normative goal is, because that
